# Corollaries of the Second Law: Entropy {#sec-ch6}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Explain the **corollaries** of the second law of thermodynamics and their
  applications.
- Define the **absolute temperature scale** and quantify the best possible
  performance of thermodynamic cycles using the concept of **reversibility**.
- Evaluate **entropy** and its change during a process.
:::

## Introduction

The **Clausius statement** of the second law, introduced in the last chapter, is
considered as the first corollary of the second law. In this chapter we discuss
corollaries 2 to 8. Each one is built on the ones before it, and together they
take us from the second law, stated for cycles, to a new system property,
**entropy**, which lets us apply the second law to any process.

![The corollaries of the second law, step by step. C1 is the Clausius statement of CH5; this chapter climbs from C2 to C8.](figures/img/ch6-corollaries.png){width=90%}

## Reversible thermodynamic cycles

Corollaries 2 and 3 are about **reversible** (i.e. ideal) thermodynamic cycles,
and they are often called the **Carnot corollaries**.

![](figures/img/ch6-carnot.png){width=22% fig-align="center"}

::: {.key}
**Corollary 2:** It is *impossible* to construct a heat engine operating between
only two heat reservoirs that will have a higher efficiency than a *reversible*
engine operating between the same two reservoirs.
:::

**Proof.** Suppose that the reverse is true: an imaginary engine I has a higher
efficiency than a reversible engine R, $\eta_I > \eta_R$, both working between
the same two reservoirs. Because R is reversible, we can run it backwards, as a
heat pump, and let the imaginary engine drive it.

![I: the imaginary engine, with $\eta_I > \eta_R$. R: the reversible engine, run backwards. Both exchange the same $|Q_H|$ with the hot reservoir.](figures/out/ch6-carnot-proof.svg){width=62%}

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Same $|Q_H|$ for both; $\eta_I > \eta_R$ means $|W_I| > |W_R|$."}
Let both engines exchange the same heat $|Q_H|$ with the hot reservoir. Since
$\eta = |W|/|Q_H|$,
$$
\eta_I > \eta_R
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|W_I| = \eta_I |Q_H| \;>\; |W_R| = \eta_R |Q_H|
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Run R backwards: it takes $|W_R|$ (supplied by I) and returns $|Q_H|$ to the hot reservoir."}
Run R backwards: it takes $|Q_{C,R}|$ from the cold reservoir, receives the work
$|W_R|$ (supplied by I) and delivers $|Q_H|$ to the hot reservoir. The hot
reservoir therefore gets back exactly what I took from it: **no net heat
exchange with the hot reservoir**.
:::

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Net effect of I + R: work $|W_I| - |W_R| > 0$ out, all of it drawn as heat from the COLD reservoir only."}
The combined device I + R still delivers the net work $|W_I| - |W_R| > 0$. By
the first law for the two cycles together, that energy must come from the only
reservoir it still exchanges heat with, the cold one:
$$
|Q_{C,R}| - |Q_{C,I}| = |W_I| - |W_R| > 0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="One reservoir, net work out: violates Kelvin–Planck, so the assumption is false."}
So the combined device exchanges heat with a **single** reservoir and produces
net work. This violates the Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law, so the
assumption $\eta_I > \eta_R$ must be false.
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\eta \le \eta_\text{rev}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\eta_\text{max} = \eta_\text{rev}
$$
:::

::: {.note}
Likewise, one can prove that any reversible refrigerator (or heat pump) has the
maximum theoretical coefficient of performance (COP):
$$
\beta_\text{max} = \left(\frac{|Q_C|}{|W|}\right)_\text{max} = \beta_\text{rev},
\qquad
\beta'_\text{max} = \left(\frac{|Q_H|}{|W|}\right)_\text{max} = \beta'_\text{rev}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
**Corollary 3:** All reversible heat engines operating between the same two
reservoirs have the same efficiency.
:::

![](figures/out/ch6-three-reversible.svg){width=72% fig-align="center"}

::: {.note}
As a result of corollary 3, the efficiency of a *reversible* heat engine is
**independent of the working fluid**, and it only depends on the thermal
reservoir property, namely the reservoir temperature:
$$
\eta_\text{rev} = f\left(T_H, T_C\right)
$$
:::

## Thermodynamic (absolute) temperature scale

**Relative temperature scale:** as discussed in CH1, the zeroth law of
thermodynamics provides a basis for temperature measurement in terms of a
particular thermometer substance and device.

**Thermodynamic (absolute) temperature scale:** a temperature scale that is
independent of any particular substance would be most desirable.

::: {.key}
**Corollary 4:** A scale of temperature can be defined which is independent of
any particular thermometric substance and which provides an absolute zero of
temperature ($T > 0$).
:::

By corollary 3, the efficiency of a reversible engine depends only on the two
reservoir temperatures:

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$\eta_\text{rev} = 1 - (|Q_C|/|Q_H|)_\text{rev} = f(T_H,T_C)$, so the heat ratio is itself a function of $T_H, T_C$ only."}
$$
\eta_\text{rev} = 1 - \left(\frac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|}\right)_\text{rev} = f\left(T_H, T_C\right)
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\left(\frac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|}\right)_\text{rev} = f^{*}\left(T_H, T_C\right)
$$
:::

Kelvin chose the simplest such function, which **defines** the Kelvin
(absolute) temperature scale:

::: {.key}
$$
\left(\frac{|Q_H|}{|Q_C|}\right)_\text{rev} = \frac{T_H}{T_C}
$$ {#eq-ch6-kelvin}
:::

![On the Kelvin scale the heat exchanged by a reversible engine is proportional to the reservoir temperature. Since $|Q_C| > 0$ (an engine must reject some heat), $T > 0$: absolute zero is the limit $|Q_C| \to 0$.](figures/out/ch6-kelvin-scale.svg){width=56%}

According to corollaries 2–4, the best possible performance for thermodynamic
cycles operating between two thermal reservoirs with temperatures $T_H$ and
$T_C$ is given by:

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Heat engine: substitute the Kelvin relation into $1 - (|Q_C|/|Q_H|)_\text{rev}$."}
**Heat engine:**
$$
\eta_\text{max} = \left(\frac{|W|}{|Q_H|}\right)_\text{rev}
= 1 - \left(\frac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|}\right)_\text{rev}
= 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Refrigerator: replace the heat ratio by the temperature ratio."}
**Refrigerator:**
$$
\beta_\text{max} = \left(\frac{|Q_C|}{|W|}\right)_\text{rev}
= \left(\frac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H| - |Q_C|}\right)_\text{rev}
= \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Heat pump: the same, with $|Q_H|$ on top."}
**Heat pump:**
$$
\beta'_\text{max} = \left(\frac{|Q_H|}{|W|}\right)_\text{rev}
= \left(\frac{|Q_H|}{|Q_H| - |Q_C|}\right)_\text{rev}
= \frac{T_H}{T_H - T_C}
$$
:::

These are the maximum (theoretical) efficiencies and COPs:

::: {.key}
$$
\eta_\text{max} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H},
\qquad
\beta_\text{max} = \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C},
\qquad
\beta'_\text{max} = \frac{T_H}{T_H - T_C}
$$ {#eq-ch6-max-performance}
with $T_H$ and $T_C$ in **kelvin**.
:::

::: {.example}
Consider a heat engine, a refrigerator and a heat pump all operating between the
same hot and cold reservoirs with temperatures 400 K and 200 K, respectively. If
they are **reversible**, calculate the heat engine thermal efficiency and the
COP of the refrigerator and the heat pump.

![](figures/img/ch6-example-devices.png){width=80% fig-align="center"}

**Step 1.** *Heat engine: use $\eta_\text{rev} = 1 - T_C/T_H$.*

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="$1 - 200/400 = 50\%$."}
$$
\eta_\text{rev} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{200}{400} = \boxed{50\%}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *Refrigerator: use $\beta_\text{rev} = T_C/(T_H - T_C)$.*

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="$200/(400-200) = 1$."}
$$
\beta_\text{rev} = \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C} = \frac{200}{400 - 200} = \boxed{1}
$$
:::

**Step 3.** *Heat pump: use $\beta'_\text{rev} = T_H/(T_H - T_C)$. How is the
answer related to Step 2?*

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$400/(400-200) = 2$; note $\beta' = \beta + 1$."}
$$
\beta'_\text{rev} = \frac{T_H}{T_H - T_C} = \frac{400}{400 - 200} = \boxed{2}
$$
Note that $\beta' = \beta + 1$.
:::
:::

## Cycle operating between more than two thermal reservoirs

::: {.key}
**Corollary 5:** The efficiency of a reversible heat engine operating between
several reservoirs must be less than that of a reversible heat engine operating
between the highest and the lowest reservoir temperatures.
:::

![](figures/out/ch6-multi-reservoir.svg){width=44% fig-align="center"}

From corollary 4, $\eta_\text{rev} = 1 - T_C/T_H$.

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Heat is taken in at temperatures up to max$(T_H)$ and rejected at temperatures down to min$(T_C)$: the best possible pair is max and min."}
The engine takes in heat at temperatures no higher than $\max(T_H)$ and rejects
heat at temperatures no lower than $\min(T_C)$, so
$$
\eta_\text{rev} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} \;\le\; 1 - \frac{\min(T_C)}{\max(T_H)}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\eta_{\text{rev, several reservoirs}} < 1 - \frac{T_{C,\min}}{T_{H,\max}}
$$
:::

**Practical implication:** to maximise the efficiency of a heat engine, input as
much heat as possible at the highest temperature and reject heat as much as
possible at the lowest temperature.

## Clausius inequality

::: {.key}
**Corollary 6:** For *any* cycle, $\oint (\delta Q/T)$ is zero if the cycle is
reversible and negative if irreversible. In general
$$
\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0 .
$$
:::

::: {.note}
Do not confuse the Clausius **inequality** (corollary 6) with the Clausius
**statement** of the second law (CH5).
:::

**Proof.**

![](figures/img/ch6-heat-engine.png){width=18% fig-align="right"}

**For a reversible heat engine.** Heat crosses the boundary only at the two
reservoirs, each at a constant temperature; $Q_H > 0$ and $Q_C < 0$.

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Two heat transfers, each at constant $T$; $Q_C$ is negative. Label (I)."}
$$
\oint \frac{\delta Q_\text{rev}}{T}
= \frac{Q_H}{T_H} + \frac{Q_C}{T_C}
= \frac{|Q_H|}{T_H} - \frac{|Q_C|}{T_C} \tag{I}
$$
:::

From corollary 4:
$$
\left(\frac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|}\right)_\text{rev} = \frac{T_C}{T_H} \tag{II}
$$

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="(II) says $|Q_H|/T_H = |Q_C|/T_C$; put it in (I)."}
From (I) and (II), $|Q_H|/T_H = |Q_C|/T_C$, so
$$
\oint \frac{\delta Q_\text{rev}}{T} = 0
$$
:::

**For an irreversible heat engine.** Compare it with a reversible engine taking
the same $|Q_H|$ from the same hot reservoir:

![](figures/out/ch6-rev-irrev.svg){width=52% fig-align="center"}

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="By corollary 2 the irreversible engine does less work, so it must reject more heat."}
By corollary 2, the irreversible engine is less efficient, so with the same
$|Q_H|$ it does less work and, by the first law, rejects more heat:
$$
|W'| < |W|
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
|Q_C'| > |Q_C|
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Irreversible sum: the second term is bigger than in the reversible case, whose sum is zero."}
$$
\oint \frac{\delta Q_\text{ir}}{T}
= \underbrace{\frac{|Q_H|}{T_H} - \frac{|Q_C'|}{T_C}}_\text{irrev}
\;<\;
\underbrace{\frac{|Q_H|}{T_H} - \frac{|Q_C|}{T_C}}_\text{rev} = 0
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\oint \frac{\delta Q_\text{rev}}{T} = 0,
\qquad
\oint \frac{\delta Q_\text{ir}}{T} < 0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} \le 0
$$
:::

::: {.note}
The Clausius inequality is valid for **all possible cycles**, including
*reversible* and *irreversible* heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps.
:::

## A new system property: entropy

::: {.key}
**Corollary 7:** There exists a property of a closed system such that a change
in its value between state 1 and state 2 during any **reversible process** is
equal to $\int (\delta Q/T)$.
:::

**Proof.** From corollary 6, for a reversible cycle,
$\oint (\delta Q_\text{rev}/T) = 0$. Take two states 1 and 2, a reversible
process $a$ from 1 to 2, and two different reversible processes $b$ and $c$
back from 2 to 1.

![](figures/out/ch6-cor7-paths.svg){width=44% fig-align="center"}

::: {.note}
**Reminder:** a quantity is a *system property* if its change in value between
two states is *independent* of the process.
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Cycle $ab$ ($1 \to 2$ along $a$, back along $b$) is reversible: its integral is zero."}
**Cycle $ab$:**
$$
\int \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_a + \int \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_b = 0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Cycle $ac$ is also reversible: zero too."}
**Cycle $ac$:**
$$
\int \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_a + \int \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_c = 0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Subtract: the $a$ terms cancel."}
Subtracting, the $a$ terms cancel:
$$
\int \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_b = \int \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_c
$$
:::

::: {.key}
For any two reversible processes between the same two states,
$\int \left(\delta Q/T\right)_b = \int \left(\delta Q/T\right)_c$: the value
depends only on the end states, so it is the change of a **system property**.
:::

If this property is denoted by **S**, this corollary can be expressed
mathematically as

::: {.key}
$$
S_2 - S_1 = \int_1^2 \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_\text{rev}
\qquad \left[\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{K}}\right]
$$ {#eq-ch6-entropy}
:::

The property $S$ is called **entropy**, with the SI unit of J/K. The **specific
entropy** ($s$) is defined as:

::: {.key}
$$
s_2 - s_1 = \frac{S_2 - S_1}{m} = \int_1^2 \left(\frac{\delta q}{T}\right)_\text{rev}
\qquad \left[\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}\right]
$$
:::

::: {.note}
The change of entropy is equal to $\int (\delta Q/T)$ **ONLY** during a
*reversible* process. In general, the value of entropy at each state can be
determined as a function of two other independent system properties (e.g. $T$,
$P$, $u$ and $h$), regardless of the nature of the process:
$$
S = f(T, P, \ldots)
$$
:::

## Entropy change in reversible processes

We initially stated the second law for a cycle, but we found that the second law
(corollary 7) leads to a property, **entropy** ($S$), that enables us to treat
the second law quantitatively for *reversible* processes:
$$
S_2 - S_1 = \int_1^2 \left(\frac{\delta Q}{T}\right)_\text{rev}
$$
On a differential basis:

::: {.key}
$$
\mathrm{d}S = \frac{\delta Q_\text{rev}}{T}
$$
:::

![A reversible process is a quasi-equilibrium one: the path is a succession of equilibrium states, each with its own value of $S$.](figures/out/ch6-quasi-equilibrium.svg){width=36%}

### Isentropic processes

**Isentropic** means *no change* in entropy ($\mathrm{d}S = 0$). Therefore, a
**reversible adiabatic** process is an isentropic process.

**Reminder:** from CH3, we know that for an *ideal gas* undergoing an
isentropic (i.e. reversible adiabatic) process:

::: {.key}
$$
P v^{\gamma} = \text{const.},
\qquad
T v^{\gamma - 1} = \text{const.},
\qquad
P T^{\gamma/(1-\gamma)} = \text{const.},
\qquad
\gamma = \frac{c_p}{c_v}
$$
:::

Each form follows from the first by eliminating one variable with $Pv = RT$.

### Temperature–entropy (T–S) diagram

For a *reversible* process, the area under the path shown in the
temperature–entropy (T–S) diagram is equal to the amount of heat transfer:
$$
\delta Q_\text{rev} = T\,\mathrm{d}S
$$

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Integrate both sides from 1 to 2; the left side is $Q_\text{rev}$."}
$$
\underbrace{\int_1^2 \delta Q_\text{rev}}_{Q_\text{rev}} = \int_1^2 T\,\mathrm{d}S
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
Q_\text{rev} = \int_1^2 T\,\mathrm{d}S
= \text{area under the path in the } T\text{–}S \text{ diagram}
$$
:::

![The T–S diagram does for heat what the P–V diagram does for work: for a reversible process, the area under the path on a P–V diagram is $|W|_\text{rev}$, and on a T–S diagram it is $|Q|_\text{rev}$.](figures/out/ch6-areas.svg){width=86%}

::: {.example}
A **Carnot cycle** is an ideal cycle consisting of four processes: two
**reversible isothermal** processes and two **reversible adiabatic** (i.e.
isentropic) processes. Plot this cycle in a T–s diagram.

![](figures/img/ch6-carnot-pv.png){width=30% fig-align="center"}

**Step 1.** *On the P–v diagram, which processes are the isotherms and which are
the adiabats? Where is heat added and removed, and what is the area enclosed?*

::: {.gap height="22mm" hint="2–3 isotherm at $T_H$: $Q_H$ in. 4–1 isotherm at $T_C$: $Q_C$ out. 1–2, 3–4 adiabatic, $Q = 0$. Enclosed area $= |W|_\text{cycle}$."}
- 2–3: isothermal at $T_H$, heat $Q_H$ is added.
- 4–1: isothermal at $T_C$, heat $Q_C$ is rejected.
- 1–2 and 3–4: adiabatic, $Q = 0$.

The area enclosed by the cycle on the P–v diagram is $|W|_\text{cycle}$.
:::

**Step 2.** *What shape does an isothermal process have on a T–s diagram? And
an isentropic one? Sketch the cycle.*

::: {.gap height="55mm" hint="Isothermal = horizontal line, isentropic = vertical line: the Carnot cycle is a rectangle."}
An isothermal process is a **horizontal** line ($T$ = const.) and an isentropic
process a **vertical** line ($s$ = const.), so the Carnot cycle is a
**rectangle**:

![](figures/out/ch6-carnot-ts.svg){width=56% fig-align="center"}
:::

**Step 3.** *Use the areas under the paths to link the heat and the net work.*

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Area under 2–3 is $|Q_H|$, under 4–1 is $|Q_C|$; the difference is the enclosed rectangle."}
The area under 2–3 is $|Q_H|$ and the area under 4–1 is $|Q_C|$, so the
enclosed rectangle is
$$
|W|_\text{cycle} = |Q_H| - |Q_C| = |Q|_\text{cycle}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.note}
The magnitude of the **net heat transfer** for any *reversible* cycle is equal
to the area enclosed by the cycle in the T–S diagram. According to the first law
of thermodynamics, $\sum W + \sum Q = 0$, this area should be equal to the area
enclosed by the cycle in a P–V diagram (i.e. the net cyclic work).
:::

## Corollary 8: entropy change in ANY process

::: {.key}
**Corollary 8:** For a closed system undergoing *any process* from state 1 to
state 2:
$$
S_2 - S_1 \ge \int_1^2 \frac{\delta Q}{T}
$$
with "$=$" for a reversible process (corollary 7) and "$>$" for an irreversible
one.
:::

**Proof.** From the Clausius inequality (corollary 6),
$\oint (\delta Q/T) \le 0$. Go from 1 to 2 by any process $a$, and return from 2
to 1 by a reversible process $b$.

![](figures/out/ch6-cor8-paths.svg){width=44% fig-align="center"}

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Clausius inequality for the cycle $a + b$."}
$$
\oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} = \int \frac{\delta Q_a}{T} + \int \frac{\delta Q_b}{T} \le 0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="$b$ is reversible, from 2 to 1: its integral is $S_1 - S_2$ (corollary 7)."}
Process $b$ is reversible and goes from 2 to 1, so by corollary 7
$$
\int \frac{\delta Q_b}{T} = S_1 - S_2
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Substitute and rearrange."}
$$
\Rightarrow\quad
\int \frac{\delta Q_a}{T} \le S_2 - S_1
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
S_2 - S_1 \ge \int_1^2 \frac{\delta Q}{T}
$$
:::

The change of entropy in *any process* can be written out in a general form as
an equality, often referred to as the **mathematical form of the second law of
thermodynamics**:

::: {.key}
$$
S_2 - S_1 = \int_1^2 \frac{\delta Q}{T} + S_\text{gen}
$$ {#eq-ch6-second-law}
:::

where $S_\text{gen}$ is the **entropy generation** in the process, due to
**irreversibilities occurring inside the system**, such as friction, free
expansion and a finite temperature difference:
$$
S_\text{gen}
\begin{cases}
= 0 & \text{reversible} \\
> 0 & \text{irreversible}
\end{cases}
$$

::: {.note}
The value of $S_\text{gen}$ **cannot be negative**. In contrast, the *change* in
entropy of the system may be positive, negative or zero: heat added moves the
state to the right on a T–s diagram, heat removed moves it to the left, and
entropy generation can only move it to the right.

![](figures/out/ch6-ts-sgen.svg){width=40% fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.warning}
**Reminder:** for an *irreversible* process, the work is NOT equal to
$-\int P\,\mathrm{d}V$, and the heat transfer is NOT equal to
$\int T\,\mathrm{d}S$. Therefore, the area underneath the path does not
represent work and heat on the P–v and T–s diagrams, respectively.
:::

![](figures/out/ch6-area-meaning.svg){width=100% fig-align="center"}

## Principle of the increase of entropy

Write the second law for both the system (A) and its surroundings (B), which
together make up the **universe**. The heat $\delta Q$ that enters one leaves
the other, across the same boundary.

![](figures/img/ch6-universe.png){width=26% fig-align="center"}

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Second law for the system A."}
**System A:**
$$
\Delta S_A = \int_1^2 \frac{\delta Q}{T} + S_{\text{gen},A}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Surroundings B: the same heat with the opposite sign."}
**Surroundings B:** the same heat, with the opposite sign:
$$
\Delta S_B = -\int_1^2 \frac{\delta Q}{T} + S_{\text{gen},B}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Add them: the heat terms cancel; both $S_\text{gen}$ are positive."}
Adding, the heat terms cancel:
$$
\Delta S_A + \Delta S_B = \underbrace{S_{\text{gen},A}}_{>0} + \underbrace{S_{\text{gen},B}}_{>0}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\Delta S_\text{universe} = S_{\text{gen},A} + S_{\text{gen},B} > 0
$$

*"The entropy of the whole universe is **not conserved**, and it constantly
increases."*
:::

### Directionality of processes

Processes occur only in such a direction that the total entropy of the system
plus surroundings increases.

**Entropy as an arrow of time:** as one goes "forward" in **time**, the second
law of thermodynamics says the **entropy** of both system and surroundings (as
an isolated system) can **only increase**.

![An egg breaks ($S_\text{gen} > 0$) but never un-breaks; a cup of coffee at 100 °C in a 20 °C room cools to 20 °C, never the reverse.](figures/img/ch6-arrow-of-time.png){width=90%}

## What is entropy? A physical interpretation

### Towards equilibrium (more probable state)

We all know that systems, left to themselves, tend to undergo processes until a
condition of equilibrium is attained. The increase of entropy principle suggests
that the total entropy increases as the state of equilibrium (more probable
state) is approached.

![Left: a ball released in a bowl oscillates and settles at the bottom, where $N$ balances $mg$. Middle: two blocks at 100 and 300 in contact end at 200 and 200 ($S_\text{gen} > 0$). Right: a gas released in one corner spreads through the whole box.](figures/img/ch6-equilibrium.png){width=92%}

### Lost opportunity to extract work

Entropy generation due to **irreversibilities** can be regarded as a lost
opportunity to extract work:

::: {.key}
$$
\underbrace{T}_{[\mathrm{K}]}\;\underbrace{S_\text{gen}}_{[\mathrm{J/K}]} = \text{lost work}\;[\mathrm{J}]
$$
:::

### Entropy as microscopic disorder

From the microscopic (statistical thermodynamic) viewpoint, as the system moves
toward equilibrium, our knowledge of the condition of the individual particles
making up the system decreases, which corresponds to an **increase in
microscopic disorder**.

![Before the partition is removed we know each particle (e.g. the red one) is somewhere on the left; afterwards it could be anywhere in the box.](figures/img/ch6-disorder.png){width=80%}

## Gibbs equations

Gibbs equations are the result of combining the first and the second laws of
thermodynamics for a *reversible* process.

![](figures/img/ch6-gibbs.png){width=18% fig-align="center"}

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="First law (CH2) with $\delta Q_\text{rev} = T\,\mathrm{d}S$ and $\delta W_\text{rev} = -P\,\mathrm{d}V$. Label (I)."}
CH2, first law: $\delta Q_\text{rev} + \delta W_\text{rev} = \mathrm{d}U$, with
$\delta Q_\text{rev} = T\,\mathrm{d}S$ and $\delta W_\text{rev} = -P\,\mathrm{d}V$:
$$
T\,\mathrm{d}S - P\,\mathrm{d}V = \mathrm{d}U
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
T\,\mathrm{d}S = \mathrm{d}U + P\,\mathrm{d}V \tag{I}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
**First Gibbs equation:**
$$
T\,\mathrm{d}S = \mathrm{d}U + P\,\mathrm{d}V
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Differentiate $H = U + PV$. Label (II)."}
By definition, $H = U + PV$, so:
$$
\mathrm{d}H = \mathrm{d}U + P\,\mathrm{d}V + V\,\mathrm{d}P \tag{II}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Eliminate $\mathrm{d}U + P\,\mathrm{d}V$ between (I) and (II)."}
From (I) and (II), $\mathrm{d}H = T\,\mathrm{d}S + V\,\mathrm{d}P$.
:::

::: {.key}
**Second Gibbs equation:**
$$
T\,\mathrm{d}S = \mathrm{d}H - V\,\mathrm{d}P
$$
:::

Or in specific forms:

::: {.key}
$$
T\,\mathrm{d}s = \mathrm{d}u + P\,\mathrm{d}v,
\qquad\qquad
T\,\mathrm{d}s = \mathrm{d}h - v\,\mathrm{d}P
$$
:::

::: {.note}
**Important note:** although the Gibbs equations are derived for a reversible
process, they can be used for **ANY process and system**, because their final
forms are only based on system properties: the change of entropy between two
states is the same whether the path between them is reversible or not. These two
equations are also called **thermodynamic property relations**.
:::

### Entropy change for an ideal gas

For an ideal gas, $\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T$ and $P/T = R/v$, so, from the
first Gibbs equation (with constant $c_v$):

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Divide the first Gibbs equation by $T$ and substitute $\mathrm{d}u = c_v\,\mathrm{d}T$, $P/T = R/v$."}
$$
\mathrm{d}s = \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{T} + \frac{P}{T}\,\mathrm{d}v
= c_v \frac{\mathrm{d}T}{T} + R\,\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Integrate from 1 to 2."}
$$
\int_1^2 \mathrm{d}s = c_v \int_1^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}T}{T} + R \int_1^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{v}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
s_2 - s_1 = c_v \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} + R \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1}
$$ {#eq-ch6-ds-Tv}
:::

Similarly, for an ideal gas, $\mathrm{d}h = c_p\,\mathrm{d}T$ and $v/T = R/P$,
so, from the second Gibbs equation (with constant $c_p$):

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Divide the second Gibbs equation by $T$; substitute $\mathrm{d}h = c_p\,\mathrm{d}T$, $v/T = R/P$."}
$$
\mathrm{d}s = \frac{\mathrm{d}h}{T} - \frac{v}{T}\,\mathrm{d}P
= c_p \frac{\mathrm{d}T}{T} - R\,\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{P}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Integrate from 1 to 2."}
$$
\int_1^2 \mathrm{d}s = c_p \int_1^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}T}{T} - R \int_1^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}P}{P}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
s_2 - s_1 = c_p \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} - R \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}
$$ {#eq-ch6-ds-TP}
:::

::: {.note}
@eq-ch6-ds-Tv and @eq-ch6-ds-TP are two forms of the same result: one turns into
the other with $Pv = RT$ and $c_p - c_v = R$.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

## End-of-chapter problems {#sec-ch6-problems}

::: {.tryfirst}
Have a real go at every problem here before you look at a solution. Worked
solutions are released after the lectures, but reading a solution is not the
same as being able to produce one: the time you spend stuck on a problem is
where most of the learning happens. Only once you have an answer of your own,
or have tried every approach you can think of, check it against the solution,
and compare the method, not just the final number.
:::

**P6.1 [easy].** During a process, the volume of 1 kg of air is doubled and its
pressure tripled. Find the change in specific entropy in kJ/(kg K). Assume an
ideal gas with $c_v = 0.718~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$ and
$R = 0.287~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$.

**(a)** 2.36 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 1.22 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 1.48 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 3.98

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
The change of entropy for an ideal gas:
$$
s_2 - s_1 = c_v \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} + R \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1} \tag{I}
$$

First, we need to find $T_2/T_1$. Based on the ideal-gas equation, with
$P_2/P_1 = 3$ and $v_2/v_1 = 2$:
$$
\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{P_1}\,\frac{v_2}{v_1} = 3 \times 2 = 6
$$

Now, from Eq. (I):
$$
s_2 - s_1 = 0.718~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \ln 6
          + 0.287~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \ln 2
= \boxed{1.485~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}} \quad \text{(c)}
$$
:::
:::

**P6.2 [easy].** Air in a piston–cylinder assembly undergoes a process from
state 1, where $T_1 = 400$ K, $P_1 = 200$ kPa, to state 2, where $T_2 = 600$ K,
$P_2 = 750$ kPa. Using the ideal-gas model for air, determine the change in
specific entropy between these states, in J/(kg K), if the process occurs
(i) reversibly, (ii) irreversibly. Treat air as an ideal gas with
$c_p = 1005~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$ and $R = 287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.

**(a)** 35.6, 28.1 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 28.1, 47.2 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** 33.9, 25.6 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 28.1, 28.1

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
The change of entropy for an ideal gas is given by:
$$
s_2 - s_1 = c_p \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} - R \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}
= 1005~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \ln\frac{600~\mathrm{K}}{400~\mathrm{K}}
- 287~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \ln\frac{750~\mathrm{kPa}}{200~\mathrm{kPa}}
= 28.1~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}
$$

Note that as the initial and final states for both the reversible and the
**irreversible** processes are the same, the change in entropy (as a system
property) would be the same regardless of the nature of the process:
$$
\boxed{28.1,\ 28.1~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}} \quad \text{(d)}
$$
:::
:::

**P6.3 [medium].** Find the change of specific entropy for an ideal gas that
undergoes a reversible polytropic compression (from $v_1$ to $v_2$) with a
polytropic exponent $n$. Express the answer as a function of $\ln(v_2/v_1)$, the
ratio of specific heats $\gamma$ and the polytropic exponent $n$.

**(a)** $c_v(n - \gamma)\ln(v_2/v_1)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(b)** $c_v(\gamma + n)\ln(v_2/v_1)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** $c_v(\gamma - n)\ln(v_2/v_1)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** $-c_v(\gamma + n)\ln(v_2/v_1)$

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
For an ideal gas:
$$
\Delta s = c_p \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} - R \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} \tag{I}
$$

From the ideal-gas equation:
$$
\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{P_1}\,\frac{v_2}{v_1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} + \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1} \tag{II}
$$

From (I) and (II), with $c_p - R = c_v$:
$$
\Delta s = c_p \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1} + \left(c_p - R\right) \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}
         = c_p \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1} + c_v \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} \tag{III}
$$

We also know that for a polytropic process, by definition:
$$
P_1 v_1^{\,n} = P_2 v_2^{\,n}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^{-n}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -n \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1} \tag{IV}
$$

From (III) and (IV), with $\gamma = c_p/c_v$:
$$
\Delta s = c_p \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1} - c_v n \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1}
= c_v \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1}\left(\frac{c_p}{c_v} - n\right)
= \boxed{c_v(\gamma - n)\ln\frac{v_2}{v_1}} \quad \text{(c)}
$$

**Note:** for $n = \gamma$, $\Delta s = 0$ and therefore
$Q_\text{rev} = T\Delta S = 0$, which is expected for an adiabatic process.
:::
:::

**P6.4 [medium].** Argon in a light bulb is at 90 kPa, 20 °C when it is turned
on, and electricity input now heats it to 75 °C. Find the specific entropy
change of the argon gas in kJ/(kg K). Treat argon as an ideal gas with
$c_v = 0.312~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$.

**(a)** 0.054 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 1.65 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 0.036 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 0.29

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
Entropy change for an ideal gas:
$$
\Delta s = c_v \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} + R \ln\frac{v_2}{v_1}
$$

During this process, the volume of argon in the light bulb remains constant. So
$v_2/v_1 = 1$ and $\ln(v_2/v_1) = 0$. Therefore, we have:
$$
\Delta s = c_v \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1}
= 0.312~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \ln\frac{273 + 75}{273 + 20}
= \boxed{0.054~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$

**Note:** temperature should be written in kelvin.
:::
:::

**P6.5 [hard].** Argon in a light bulb is at 110 kPa, 80 °C. The light is
turned off, so the argon cools to the ambient 20 °C. Disregard the glass and any
other mass and find the specific entropy generation $s_\text{gen}$ in
J/(kg K). (Treat argon as an ideal gas with $c_v = 0.312~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** 3.2 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 5.8 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 1.2 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 0.6

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
To find the entropy generation, we can use the second law:
$$
\Delta s = \frac{q}{T} + s_\text{gen}
$$
So we need to find $\Delta s$ and $q/T$.

![](figures/img/ch6-p-bulb-sol.png){width=30% fig-align="center"}

To find $\Delta s$ for an ideal gas, with $v_2/v_1 = 1$ (the bulb is rigid):
$$
\Delta s = c_v \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} + R \ln\underbrace{\frac{v_2}{v_1}}_{=1}
= c_v \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1}
= 0.312~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \times \ln\frac{20 + 273}{80 + 273}
= -0.0581~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}
$$

Next, we find $q/T$. From the energy equation for a closed system:
$$
q + w = \Delta u = c_v \Delta T
$$
The light is turned off, so there is no electrical work ($w = 0$). Thus:
$$
q = c_v \Delta T
= 0.312~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \left(20 - 80\right)\mathrm{K}
= -18.72~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg}}
$$

$T$ in $q/T$ is the temperature at which the heat transfer occurs, in other
words the temperature at the system boundary, which is equal to the temperature
of the surroundings. So:
$$
\Delta s = \frac{q}{T} + s_\text{gen}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
-0.0581~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}
= -\frac{18.72~\mathrm{kJ/kg}}{(273 + 20)~\mathrm{K}} + s_\text{gen}
$$
$$
\Rightarrow\quad
s_\text{gen} = 0.0058~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}
= \boxed{5.8~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}} \quad \text{(b)}
$$
:::
:::

**P6.6 [hard].** A cylinder/piston contains carbon dioxide at 1 MPa, 300 °C
with a volume of 200 L. The total external force acting on the piston is
proportional to $V^3$. This system is allowed to cool to room temperature,
20 °C. What is the entropy generation $S_\text{gen}$ for the process in kJ/K?
Treat carbon dioxide as an ideal gas with $R = 188.92~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$ and
$c_v = 653~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$, and assume that the system pressure is
infinitesimally different from the external pressure.

*Hint: this is a challenging problem. To solve it, you can first find the heat
transfer using the first law of thermodynamics. Then, find the change of entropy
for an ideal gas. That being done, you can then use the second law of
thermodynamics to find the entropy generation.*

**(a)** 0.126 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 0.589 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 0.634
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 0.366

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
To find $S_\text{gen}$ we use the second law, so we first need $S_2 - S_1$
and $\int \delta Q/T$:
$$
S_2 - S_1 = \int \frac{\delta Q}{T} + S_\text{gen} \tag{I}
$$

![](figures/img/ch6-p-co2-sol.png){width=28% fig-align="center"}

**Find $\int \delta Q/T$.** The temperature at the border of the system (where
the heat transfer occurs) is constant and equal to that of the surroundings, so
$\int \delta Q/T = Q/T_\text{surr}$. To find $Q$ we use the energy equation,
with $\Delta U = m c_v \Delta T$ for an ideal gas:
$$
Q + W = m c_v \Delta T \tag{II}
$$
The work follows from $P = P_\text{ext} = F_\text{ext}/A \propto V^{3}$, so
$PV^{-3} = \text{const.}$: a polytropic process with $n = -3$. With $PV = mRT$:
$$
m = \frac{P_1 V_1}{R T_1}
= \frac{10^{6}~\mathrm{Pa} \times 200\times10^{-3}~\mathrm{m^3}}
       {188.92~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times 573~\mathrm{K}} = 1.847~\mathrm{kg}
$$
$$
W = \frac{P_2 V_2 - P_1 V_1}{n - 1} = \frac{m R \left(T_2 - T_1\right)}{n - 1}
= \frac{1.847 \times 188.92 \times (20 - 300)}{-3 - 1} = 24.4~\mathrm{kJ} \tag{III}
$$
From (II) and (III):
$$
Q = m c_v \left(T_2 - T_1\right) - W
= 1.847 \times 0.653 \times (20 - 300) - 24.4 = -362.2~\mathrm{kJ}
$$

**Find $S_2 - S_1$.** For an ideal gas,
$$
S_2 - S_1 = m\left[c_v \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1} + R \ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right] \tag{IV}
$$
For the polytropic process, with $P = mRT/V$:
$$
\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \frac{V_2^{-n}}{V_1^{-n}}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{T_2}{T_1}\,\frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{V_2^{-n}}{V_1^{-n}}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-n}}
= \left(\frac{273 + 20}{273 + 300}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-(-3)}} = 0.846
$$
From Eq. (IV):
$$
S_2 - S_1 = 1.847~\mathrm{kg}\left[0.653~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}}
\ln\frac{293}{573}
+ 0.18892~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{kg\,K}} \ln 0.846\right]
= -0.868~\mathrm{kJ/K}
$$

**Entropy generation.** From Eq. (I):
$$
-0.868~\frac{\mathrm{kJ}}{\mathrm{K}}
= \frac{-362.2~\mathrm{kJ}}{(20 + 273)~\mathrm{K}} + S_\text{gen}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
S_\text{gen} = -0.868 + 1.236 = \boxed{0.37~\mathrm{kJ/K}} \quad \text{(d)}
$$
The listed 0.366 kJ/K is what you get if $S_2 - S_1$ is first rounded to
$-0.87$ kJ/K.
:::
:::
